gap: No result ChatGPT got states that every 16-inch MacBook Pro Apple sells today uses an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, which drives three or four external displays natively. The 'base M-chip supports one external display' caveat therefore does not apply to a 16-inch Mac, and a driver-free extender with two added screens runs both screens independently without the UsbDisplay/DisplayLink-style driver.
standout_why: Compared against UPERFECT's '8 Best Triple Screen Laptop Extenders in 2026' (cited in chat ab-17 #1), our own Dealectric page (cited in chat ab-17 #2), WorkCocoon's 'Best 16-Inch Laptop Screen Extenders' (a top result) and ChatGPT's answers. UPERFECT gives only 'base MacBook M1 and M2 chip models only support one external display'. Our page justifies the driver-based S788 by saying a base M1/M2/M3 Mac is 'limited to one native external display'. ChatGPT's third answer repeats the base-chip warning. WorkCocoon has no Mac or driver content. None of these pages works out what the 16-inch laptop in the question can actually drive. Partly overlapping caveats already exist, so this is new and useful but not unique ground.
decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro: 3 external displays; M5 Max: 4), the driver-free dual-16-inch extenders work with both screens extended and no driver. These are the FOPO S11 at $399.99 and the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite. That removes the Mac reason our page gives for picking the driver-based S788. The S788 is still the choice only for a buyer who wants three added screens, which makes four displays in total, not a triple-screen setup. For a laptop + 2 'triple' setup, the pick shifts toward the S11 or Dual Lite. The footnote for the table is: 'Triple' in product names is not a fixed count. FOPO S11 means laptop + 2 screens. FOPO S788 'Triple' means 3 added screens, so 4 displays. INVZI MagHub 'Quad Max' means 3 added screens.
